You can reach them at James.t@thegamer.com Sign in to your TheGamer account Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap PCs, consoles, phones, and all other consumer-facing tech are in crisis, as AI data centers continue to swallow global memory demand in what has been dubbed the 'RAMpocalypse.' There has been plenty of humming and hawing over when prices will finally settle and computing will become affordable again , especially as we look down the barrel of $1,000+ home consoles . Even OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is concerned... just not about consumers.

Altman argued in an interview on the Cheeky Pint podcast (via FRVR ) that the DRAM shortage isn't the fault of data centers, but people daring to have memory in their own rigs for locally-run models. In so many words, the data centers eating up supply aren't the issue, you are.

"From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everyone have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer. And be used 5% of the time," Altman said.

Altman isn't strictly talking about gamers or everyday consumers, but it's not a leap to suggest that him referring to everyone having "a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer" would apply to those groups, not just users with locally-run open-source AI models.

By his logic, having 32GB of RAM sitting in your rig for gaming is a complete waste of global supply. Why let consumers use up all that precious memory when it could be packed into a data center so that people can cheat on their homework assignments and generate deepfakes to harass women online?

“A lot of people want local inference,” Altman said. “And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now. Because we are going to have open-source models. We’re going to be able to run them on our own computers. And so we’re not going to need all the stuff [DRAM] in the data center.

“You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very constrained environment,” he continued. “And somehow everyone’s, many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”

Altman argues that "we all have a shared interest" due to the world's limited silicon capacity, and that AI will discover efficiency gains and become a vital, everyday part of computing. Except, in this hypothetical future, nobody will be able to afford computers. It's a future that many are concerned about, where, instead of having local computers, everything is run through the cloud.

YouTube If there's a sliver of hope, though, it's that the AI bubble is finally starting to pop.

Investors are growing cautious , US Democrats have proposed a bill to withhold bailouts for bankrupt AI firms , Google's value plummeted by $500 billion as its own AI summaries eat into traditional search ad revenue, and China's AI bubble has already burst . With giants like OpenAI and Anthropic burning through billions a year, Altman's dream of a world where data centers hoard every stick of memory and consumers get the scraps feels like a pipe dream.

Gamers in 2000 were just as confused and annoyed at Tim Sweeney's awful takes.

In an interview over beers with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint, Altman said that local inference, and, by extension, people having DRAM in computers at home, is "quite terrible."

When discussing local inference on home computers with open-source models, Altman discussed the assumption that people will be able to run local AI on their own computers, the ones they may already own or want to build. Then he explained why that's a bad idea (at the 29-minute mark):

"From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used 5% of the time," Altman said. "You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you're trying to deal with this very supply-constrained environment. And somehow many people's intuition is the opposite of that."

While OpenAI does have some open-source models, its primary business is in closed-source models that run in data centers, so he's really defending the company's business model.

Watch On OpenAI isn't exactly threatened by some laptops and gaming rigs just yet, but local AI could mean people one day paying less for subscriptions to models like GPT-6 Luna if they have the power to run them at home. Altman's talk suggests that the company would prefer that more RAM go to OpenAI's data centers rather than home computers, which also sparks enthusiast fears of not being able to own your own hardware or software, but rather rent an agent and a computer in the cloud. Some of what Altman is saying is based on an idea that data center buildouts won't slow down. It also assumes that RAM being used in AI data centers 24/7 is more worthwhile than RAM that is used for spreadsheets, web browsing, gaming, and maybe even local AI occasionally. The rest of the wide-ranging interview includes talk of this week's PHP vulnerabilities, sandboxing models in training, and OpenAI's research in mathematics.
